title: Isaiah 53 was read messianically in the rabbis' own literature
claim: The claim that only Christians read Isaiah 52:13–53:12 of an individual Messiah is contradicted by classical Jewish sources. Targum Jonathan — the official Aramaic paraphrase — opens the passage 'Behold, my servant the Messiah shall prosper' (on Isa 52:13). The Talmud, asking the Messiah's name, answers 'the leper scholar of the house of Rabbi,' citing Isaiah 53:4 — 'surely he has borne our griefs' (Sanhedrin 98b). Ruth Rabbah 5:6 applies Isaiah 53:5 to the Messiah's sufferings. A Yom Kippur Musaf piyyut ('Az milifnei bereshit,' preserved in old Ashkenazi machzorim) speaks of 'our righteous anointed' who 'carries our sins.' The 16th-century commentator Moshe Alshich wrote that 'our rabbis with one voice' applied the passage to King Messiah. None of this proves Jesus is that Messiah — but it establishes that an individual, even suffering, messianic reading of Isaiah 53 is native to Jewish tradition, not a Christian import.
rabbinic: Yom Kippur Musaf piyyut 'Az milifnei bereshit'

sources.name: Michael Brown, Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus, vol. 3
Tovia Singer, 'Who is God's Suffering Servant?'

response: Rabbi Tovia Singer and Jews for Judaism respond that citing these texts is selective. The Targum applies the servant's EXALTATION to Messiah but systematically reroutes the suffering onto Israel and the nations — it is evidence against, not for, a suffering Messiah. Aggadic passages like Sanhedrin 98b are homiletical wordplay, not exegesis; midrash routinely applies verses to many figures without fixing their plain meaning (peshat). The dominant medieval exegetical tradition — Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak — reads the servant as Israel, consistent with Isaiah's repeated 'Israel, my servant' (41:8; 44:1; 49:3). A tradition's homiletics do not overturn its exegesis.

responseSource.name: Tovia Singer, Outreach Judaism; Jews for Judaism counter-missionary materials

rationale: The narrow fact is conceded on all sides: messianic (including suffering-messianic) readings of Isaiah 53 exist inside pre-modern Jewish literature — the debate is over their weight, not their existence. Use it exactly that way: not 'the rabbis agree with us,' but 'an individual-Messiah reading of this chapter is a Jewish option, attested in Jewish sources, so considering it is not conversion to a foreign idea.' Concede the Targum's rerouting of the suffering honestly — overclaiming it will be caught instantly by anyone who has read Singer. This entry opens the door; the textual case lives in the companion entry.

plain.d: Isaiah 53 is in the Old Testament. It describes a man God calls "my servant." He is hated. He is wounded. He is killed and buried. Then, somehow, he lives and is satisfied. Christians have pointed at this chapter for two thousand years.

plain.t: What your Jewish friend will say back
plain.d: That the servant is the nation of Israel, not one man. Israel suffered at the hands of other nations. So the chapter is about a people. This is the standard Jewish answer today, and it is a serious one.

plain.t: The part almost no Christian knows
plain.d: That answer became standard fairly late — after Rashi, a French rabbi, around 1100 AD. Before him, Jewish sources read the chapter as being about the Messiah. The clearest example is the Targum, the old Aramaic version that was read aloud in synagogues. It begins: "Behold, my servant the Messiah shall prosper."
Very strong, because you are not using a Christian source. You are pointing at a Jewish one. Your friend can look it up without trusting you at all.

It changes what kind of conversation you are having. You are not telling a Jewish person what their own book means. You are asking a question about their own tradition. Those two things land completely differently.
"Have you ever read what the Targum says about Isaiah 53? I'd like to look at it with you."

title: In Isaiah 53 the servant suffers for 'my people' — he is distinguished from Israel
claim: Within the fourth Servant Song itself, the servant cannot simply be the nation. He suffers 'for the transgression of my people' (53:8) — the servant and the people are two parties, not one. He is innocent: 'he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth' (53:9), while Isaiah's Israel is confessedly sinful (1:4; 42:24-25; 53:6 'all we like sheep have gone astray'). He is silent under affliction (53:7), while Israel's laments are anything but silent. He dies — 'cut off out of the land of the living,' assigned a grave (53:8-9) — yet afterward 'prolongs his days,' while the Tanakh promises Israel never dies as a people (Jer 31:35-37). And his suffering is vicarious and effective: 'by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; he shall bear their iniquities' (53:11). Earlier songs already distinguish a servant with a mission TO Israel (49:5-6). The portrait is an innocent individual who dies for the sins of others and is exalted.
rabbinic: Origen, Contra Celsum 1.55 (attesting the collective reading in the 3rd c.)

sources.name: Jews for Judaism, 'Isaiah 53 and the Suffering Servant'
Michael Brown, Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus, vol. 3

response: The strongest counter (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Singer): Isaiah has already named the servant — 'Israel, my servant' (41:8; 44:1; 49:3) — so the burden is on the individual reading. The speakers of chapter 53 are the gentile KINGS of 52:15, astonished at Israel's vindication; each king's 'my people' (53:8) is his own nation, dissolving the servant/people distinction. 'Because of (מִן) our transgressions' (53:5) means Israel suffered from the nations' sins, not vicariously for them. National Israel 'dies' and revives in exile imagery (Ezekiel 37's dry bones), and the innocent-sufferer language fits the righteous remnant. This reading is not a medieval invention — Origen's Jewish interlocutors argued it c. 248 AD.

responseSource.name: Rashi on Isaiah 53; Tovia Singer, 'The Suffering Servant of Isaiah 53' (Outreach Judaism)

rationale: Graded unrefuted on the narrow textual claim: the collective reading must make the kings the penitent confessors and 'my people' distributive — readings that strain 53:8-9 (an individual grave with 'a rich man in his death') and reverse the passage's grammar of substitution ('HE was wounded for OUR transgressions... the LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all'). Note honestly: critical scholars remain divided on the servant's identity, and Origen proves the collective reading predates Rashi — never claim Rashi invented it in the 1100s. Use as a slow shared reading of the Hebrew, verse by verse, asking only: who is the 'he,' who is the 'we'? Let the text do the work.

plain.d: If the servant in Isaiah 53 is the nation of Israel, the Christian reading of the chapter collapses. So everything turns on one question. Does the chapter treat the servant as the nation, or as someone separate from it?

plain.t: The verse that does the work
plain.d: Isaiah 53:8 says the servant was struck "for the transgression of my people." Read that slowly. The servant is punished for the people. So he cannot be the people. A nation cannot be punished for its own sins on its own behalf.

Isaiah 53:9 says he had "done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth." The prophets never say that about Israel. They say the opposite, over and over, at length. Isaiah himself does it in chapter 1.

plain.t: Where the other side has a point
plain.d: Isaiah does call Israel God's servant elsewhere — in Isaiah 41:8, Isaiah 44:1 and Isaiah 49:3. That is true, and you should say so first. The word "servant" alone proves nothing. The argument has to come from chapter 53 itself.
Strong. Counter-missionary writers — the Jewish teachers who answer Christian claims — usually move to those other chapters instead of dealing with 53:8. Ask about 53:8 and then stop talking.
"Read me Isaiah 53:8. Who is the servant being struck for?"

title: The rabbis' own two-Messiah doctrine concedes the two portraits
claim: The Tanakh contains two messianic portraits that resist merging: a reigning Davidic king (Isa 9:6-7; 11; Jer 23:5-6; Zech 9:9-10) and a suffering, pierced, dying figure (Isa 53; Zech 12:10; Ps 22; Dan 9:26). Rabbinic Judaism itself saw both and answered with TWO Messiahs: Messiah ben Joseph, who fights and is slain — the Talmud applies the mourning of Zechariah 12:10-12 to his death (Sukkah 52a) — and Messiah ben David, who then reigns. Later midrash goes further: Pesikta Rabbati 36-37 portrays a Messiah ('Ephraim, our righteous Messiah') who accepts crushing sufferings for the sins of Israel. The two-Messiah scheme is the tradition's own admission that the sources present both a slain sufferer and a triumphant king. Christianity's claim is structurally parallel and more economical: one Messiah, two comings — suffering servant first, returning king second (Luke 24:26; Heb 9:28).

sources.name: Michael Brown, Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus, vol. 2

response: The rabbinic response: Messiah ben Joseph is a WARRIOR who dies in the eschatological battle against Gog — he is not an atoning sacrifice, his death accomplishes nothing redemptive, and he dies at the END of history, not centuries before the redemption. The concept is post-biblical, marginal, and possibly a response to Bar Kokhba's death (132-135 AD), not ancient doctrine. Above all, Maimonides' test stands (Mishneh Torah, Melachim 11): the Messiah is identified by what he accomplishes — rebuilt temple, ingathered exiles, world peace, universal knowledge of God. A candidate who dies without accomplishing these is thereby disqualified; positing a second coming is an unfalsifiable patch, and the rabbis' two Messiahs at least both act within the one redemption.

responseSource.name: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Melachim uMilchamot 11:3-4; Tovia Singer, Outreach Judaism

rationale: The admitted core: the tradition itself found a slain messianic figure in the texts — Sukkah 52a hangs his death on Zechariah 12:10, the same verse John 19:37 cites. Boyarin (a Talmud professor, no Christian) argues suffering-Messiah ideas are Jewish to the bone. Use it to reframe the whole conversation: the question was never 'does the Tanakh have a suffering Messiah?' — Jewish sources answered yes — but 'is it one Messiah twice, or two Messiahs once?' Engage Rambam's test respectfully and head-on: the unfinished tasks are exactly what the NT assigns to the return (Acts 3:21). Never deploy this as 'gotcha, your own Talmud' — it is common ground, not a trap.

plain.t: The problem sitting in the text
plain.d: The Old Testament seems to describe the coming one twice, in two ways that do not fit together. One is a king from David's family who wins and rules in peace. The other is a servant who is hated, pierced and killed. Both pictures are there.

This is not something Christians spotted. The Talmud — the huge Jewish collection of rabbinic teaching, finished around 500 AD — hits the same problem. Its answer, in a passage called Sukkah 52a, is two Messiahs. Messiah son of Joseph suffers and is killed. Messiah son of David reigns.
Less than it sounds. Not two people, but one person, twice. He came first as the servant. He returns as the king. Every piece of the rabbis' own solution is kept. Only the counting changes.
Very strong. The two-picture problem is admitted inside Judaism, in one of its own central books. You are not inventing the difficulty.
It stops the conversation being "my book versus your book." You are both looking at the same puzzle in the same text. You just solve it differently.
"Why is one person coming twice harder to believe than two different Messiahs?"

title: Daniel 9: an anointed one is cut off before the Second Temple's destruction
claim: Daniel 9:24-27 sets seventy 'weeks' for Israel and Jerusalem 'to finish transgression... to atone for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness.' The load-bearing anchor needs no precise chronology: 'an anointed one shall be cut off and have nothing; and the people of the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary' (9:26). Whatever the counting scheme, the mashiach is cut off BEFORE the destruction — which occurred in 70 AD. So the window closed in 70 AD. Strikingly, the traditional Jewish chronology agrees on the terminus: Seder Olam Rabbah runs the 490 years to the Second Temple's destruction, and Rashi identifies the cut-off anointed one with Agrippa at the destruction. Jesus of Nazareth was cut off c. 30-33 AD, within the final generation of the standing temple, followed by the destruction — matching the sequence. Josephus (War 6.312-313) attests that an 'ambiguous oracle' in the scriptures fueled first-century expectation that the time had come.

sources.name: Michael Brown, Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus, vol. 1

response: Two-layer counter. Rabbinic: 'mashiach' means any anointed one — Rashi reads v.25's anointed as Cyrus and v.26's as King Agrippa; the passage concerns the temple era, not a dying redeemer, and the Talmud curses end-date calculators ('blasted be the bones of those who calculate the end,' Sanhedrin 97b) precisely because such reckonings breed false messiahs. Critical-scholarly (the stronger form): Daniel 9 was composed in the 160s BC; the anointed one 'cut off' is the high priest Onias III, murdered in 171 BC, and the desolator is Antiochus IV — the seventy weeks end in the Maccabean crisis, and the Christian count requires cherry-picking a start decree and treating symbolic sabbatical numbers as exact solar arithmetic.

responseSource.name: Rashi on Daniel 9; Sanhedrin 97b; John J. Collins, Daniel (Hermeneia)

rationale: Graded contested because the Maccabean reading is the critical consensus and deserves the respect of being named. But the usable core survives every reading a Jewish interlocutor is likely to hold: on the TRADITIONAL chronology (Seder Olam, Rashi), the seventy weeks terminate at 70 AD — so by the tradition's own math, whatever the passage promised ('atone for iniquity, everlasting righteousness') belongs to the era that ended with the destruction. Use it as a question, not an equation: 'On your own sources' timeline, what happened in that window?' Avoid decree-arithmetic showdowns (458 vs 444 BC) — the anchor 'cut off before the destruction' is the whole argument. Never mock the Sanhedrin 97b curse; acknowledge its pastoral wisdom about false messiahs.

plain.d: Almost any prophecy can be placed somewhere in history if you push hard enough. That is why arguing about them rarely settles anything. Daniel 9 is different. It puts events in a fixed order, and the last one has already happened.

Daniel 9:26 says an anointed one shall be "cut off, but not for himself." Then it says the people of a coming ruler shall "destroy the city and the sanctuary." The sanctuary is the Temple in Jerusalem. Rome burned it in AD 70.

The maths of Daniel's "seventy weeks" is genuinely argued about. There are several ways to count them and no agreement, even among Christians. Do not pretend there is. But the order does not depend on the maths. Cut off first. Temple destroyed second.
Contested, and say that. The order of events is strong. The date maths is not settled. Lead with the order and give away the maths before anyone asks.
It is the only prophecy here with a deadline that has already passed. That makes it checkable in a way the others are not — and Daniel is a book your friend already accepts.
"Daniel 9:26 has someone cut off before the Temple is destroyed. The Temple fell in AD 70. Who was that?"

title: Micah 5:2 — the ruler from Bethlehem whose origins are from of old
claim: Micah 5:2 (5:1 in Hebrew editions): 'You, Bethlehem Ephrathah, little among the clans of Judah — from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose origins are from of old, from ancient days.' The messianic identification is not contested ground between Judaism and Christianity: Targum Jonathan renders 'from you shall come forth before Me the Messiah,' and Rashi on the verse writes 'from you shall emerge for Me Messiah son of David.' The Gospels record that this was the standing Jewish answer to where Messiah would be born (Matt 2:4-6; John 7:42). Jesus's birth in Bethlehem is attested by both independent birth narratives (Matthew 2; Luke 2). The phrase 'origins from of old, from ancient days' (motza'otav mikedem, mimei olam) points beyond mere ancestry for Christian readers, cohering with the child called 'mighty God' in Isaiah 9:6 and the pre-existent son of Psalm 110:1.
rabbinic: Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 2:4 (Messiah and Bethlehem legend)

sources.name: Raymond Brown, The Birth of the Messiah

response: The counter-missionary reading: Micah names Bethlehem as the CLAN SEAT of David's line — 'from you' addresses the family stock (Ephrathah, cf. Ruth 4:11; 1 Sam 17:12), so the verse predicts a ruler of Davidic descent, not a birthplace requirement; 'origins from of old' means precisely that his lineage reaches back to David's ancient house, not pre-existence. Moreover, the application to Jesus is unverifiable: the two birth narratives diverge (a Herod-era flight to Egypt vs. a Quirinius census a decade later), the census mechanism is historically doubtful, and skeptics argue Bethlehem was written in BECAUSE the prophecy was known. Davidic genealogy through Joseph is moot if Joseph is not the father.

responseSource.name: Tovia Singer, Outreach Judaism; critical discussion in Raymond Brown, The Birth of the Messiah

rationale: The identification (this verse = Messiah) is admitted by the classical Jewish sources themselves — that part is solid and worth establishing, since it means messianic prophecy with checkable content exists and both traditions know it. What is genuinely contested is the application to Jesus, which rests on the historicity of the infancy narratives — a real debate; do not wave it away. Use the verse to establish the shared framework ('your sources and mine agree what this predicts'), present the double attestation of Matthew and Luke honestly alongside their tensions, and let 'origins from of old' be suggestive rather than a proof of deity. Overclaiming here costs credibility needed elsewhere.

plain.d: Micah wrote in the 700s BC. Micah 5:2 says a ruler over Israel will come out of Bethlehem Ephratah, and calls the town small — which it was. Then it adds that his "goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting."
One is about a place: this ruler comes from Bethlehem. The other is about time: he existed before he was born. The first is simple and hard to argue with. The second is where all the disagreement is.

plain.t: What your friend will say back
plain.d: That the Hebrew phrase means an ancient family line, not existence from eternity. So the verse would be saying his ancestry goes back a long way — to David, and to Judah. That is a fair reading of the words, and the Hebrew can carry it.
Contested. The Bethlehem part is solid. The "from everlasting" part is a real translation debate. A Christian who pretends it is obvious will get corrected and lose the room.
Used gently it adds weight to the whole picture. Used as a knockout punch it hands your friend an easy win.
"How do you read the second half of Micah 5:2? I've heard it taken two ways."

title: Zechariah 12:10 — Jerusalem mourns one who was pierced; the Talmud says it is a slain Messiah
claim: Zechariah 12:10 in the Masoretic Text: 'They shall look to me whom they have pierced (daqaru), and they shall mourn for him as one mourns for an only son, and grieve bitterly for him as one grieves for a firstborn.' The oscillation 'look to ME... mourn for HIM' sits in the Hebrew itself. The decisive datum comes from the Talmud: Sukkah 52a asks what the great mourning of Zechariah 12:11-12 is for, and the accepted answer applies it to Messiah ben Joseph WHO IS SLAIN, citing this very verse — 'and they shall look upon me because they have thrust him through.' So the classical Jewish reading closest to the text's plain force already saw here a pierced, slain, mourned messianic figure. John 19:37 applies the verse to the crucifixion; Revelation 1:7 to the return. The prophecy's setting — the house of David and Jerusalem's inhabitants looking in repentant grief on one they pierced, with a fountain 'opened for sin and impurity' in the next verse (13:1) — matches the Christian claim with uncanny economy.

sources.name: Michael Brown, Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus, vol. 3

response: The steelmanned counter (Singer, Rashi, and the NJPS translation): the speaker is God ('they shall look to Me'), who cannot be pierced; daqar here means slain in battle, and the verse describes end-time national mourning over those who fell in the war of Gog and Magog — NJPS renders 'they shall lament to Me about those who are slain.' The grammar 'et asher' can mean 'concerning him whom,' so no God-pierced paradox exists. Rashi's second comment does cite the Messiah ben Joseph tradition, but as aggadah about a warrior slain at history's end — not an atoning death in the Roman era. Some Hebrew manuscripts even read 'look to him (elav),' removing the Christian pivot entirely.

responseSource.name: Rashi on Zechariah 12:10; NJPS translation; Tovia Singer, Outreach Judaism

rationale: Graded admitted on the key fact: the Talmud itself connects this verse's mourning to a slain Messiah (Sukkah 52a) — the same connection John 19:37 makes. That convergence, from sources with no motive to help Christians, is the entry's entire force. Handle the me/him text question with full honesty: the MT's elai is the harder and better-attested reading, but the argument does not need it — 'mourn for HIM as for an only son' carries the individual regardless. Pair with 13:7 ('strike the shepherd') and 13:1 (the fountain for sin). Best used after the two-Messiah entry, as its sharpest concrete instance.

plain.d: Zechariah 12:10 describes a day when God pours out grace on Jerusalem. Then it says something strange: "they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him." The sentence starts with "me" and ends with "him."

plain.t: It is odd before anyone argues
plain.d: That shift is in the Hebrew itself. It is not a Christian translation trick. God is the one speaking, and yet the mourning is for someone else. Jewish commentators have wrestled with it for centuries.

plain.t: What Jewish sources make of it
plain.d: The strongest thing here is not a Christian reading. The Talmud connects this mourning to Messiah son of Joseph — the Messiah who is killed. That is the same figure from Sukkah 52a, and again it comes from inside Judaism.
Very strong, because you can make it entirely from Jewish sources. That is the only kind of argument that travels in this conversation.
A pierced figure, mourned by Jerusalem, read by Jewish sages as a Messiah who dies. That is a lot to set aside, and none of it depends on the New Testament.
"Why does Zechariah 12:10 switch from 'me' to 'him'? And what did the sages do with it?"

title: Psalm 22 — the crucifixion psalm and the kaari/kaaru textual question
claim: Psalm 22 reads like a crucifixion account written from inside: 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' (v.1, quoted by Jesus, Matt 27:46); mockers who 'shake the head' saying 'he trusted in the LORD, let him deliver him' (vv.7-8; cf. Matt 27:39-43); 'they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots' (v.18; John 19:24); ending not in death but in worldwide praise — 'all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD' (v.27). Verse 16(17) is the famous crux: the Masoretic Text reads ka'ari ('like a lion my hands and my feet' — no verb); the pre-Christian Septuagint reads 'they dug/pierced (ōryxan) my hands and feet'; and the Nahal Hever Psalms scroll (5/6HevPs, 1st century AD, a Jewish manuscript) reads the verb form ka'aru. So the 'pierced' reading is ancient and Jewish, not a Christian corruption — though its meaning is debated.

sources.name: Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library

response: The counter: ka'aru is not a known Hebrew verb for 'pierce' — the root krh means 'dig,' and 'dig my hands and feet' is strained; the MT's 'like a lion [at] my hands and feet' fits the psalm's animal imagery (bulls v.12, dogs v.16, lions vv.13,21). The psalm is David's own lament, in the past tense, with no messianic label; Midrash Tehillim applies it to Esther. The Gospel writers patterned the passion narrative ON the psalm (prophecy historicized), which explains the fit. And a telling detail: the New Testament itself NEVER quotes verse 16 — if 'they pierced my hands and feet' were the slam-dunk, the evangelists missed it. Vicarious atonement appears nowhere in the psalm.

responseSource.name: Tovia Singer, Outreach Judaism; Jews for Judaism materials on Psalm 22

rationale: Graded contested with total honesty as instructed: the textual evidence (LXX, Nahal Hever) genuinely favors an ancient verb reading and refutes the 'Christian mistranslation' charge — but 'pierced' as the verb's sense is uncertain, and the NT's silence on v.16 is a real datum an informed interlocutor will raise; concede it before they do. The psalm's power is cumulative, not lexical: mockery, the taunt quoted almost verbatim in Matthew 27:43, divided garments, and the pivot to the nations' worship. Use v.16 only to neutralize the corruption charge, never as the centerpiece. Lead with the verses the Gospels actually quote.

plain.d: Psalm 22 opens with the words Jesus quoted while dying: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" It goes on to describe a man surrounded by enemies, with his bones out of joint, mocked by watchers, and his clothing divided by lot. David wrote it centuries before crucifixion reached Judea.

Psalm 22:16 is the fight. The standard Hebrew text reads roughly "like a lion, my hands and my feet." The old Greek translation reads "they pierced my hands and my feet." One Hebrew letter separates the two, and the two letters look almost identical.

A scroll fragment found at Nahal Hever, near the Dead Sea, supports the "pierced" reading. It is about a thousand years older than the standard Hebrew text we normally use. That matters. But it is one fragment, and honest scholars still disagree.
Contested — and admitting that is the whole point here. A Christian who claims verse 16 obviously says "pierced" will be corrected, and will deserve it.
The rest of the psalm needs no argument at all. Psalm 22:7-8 has the mocking. Psalm 22:18 has the clothing divided and lots cast. Nobody disputes those verses. Give away verse 16 and read the rest.
"Let's set verse 16 aside — it's a real textual question. Read me Psalm 22:18."

title: Genesis 49:10 — the scepter of Judah and the one to whom obedience belongs
claim: Jacob's blessing: 'The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until Shiloh comes (ad ki yavo Shiloh), and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples' (Gen 49:10). The messianic identification is again native to Jewish tradition: Targum Onkelos renders 'until the Messiah comes, whose is the kingdom'; Sanhedrin 98b lists 'Shiloh' among the Messiah's names; Rashi glosses 'Shiloh — the King Messiah, to whom the kingdom belongs.' The verse thus establishes, from the Torah itself and by rabbinic consent, that Judah's line culminates in a specific individual who commands the obedience not of Israel only but of 'the peoples' (amim, plural). Christians observe that Judah's residual self-governance — the Sanhedrin's capital jurisdiction — lapsed under Rome in the generation before 70 AD (Avodah Zarah 8b records capital cases ceasing 'forty years before the destruction'), and that a son of Judah's line has in fact, uniquely in history, won the obedience of the gentile peoples.

sources.name: Michael Brown, Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus, vol. 1

response: The counter has real teeth: if 'scepter' means political sovereignty, it departed from Judah at the Babylonian exile (586 BC) and through Persian, Greek, and Hasmonean (Levite!) rule — centuries before Jesus — so the 'departed in AD 6' clock is arbitrary. Rabbinic exegesis reads shevet as tribal identity and internal authority (exilarchs, patriarchs, courts), which persisted long after 70 AD; 'ad ki' can mean 'even when,' not a terminus. And 'Shiloh' itself is obscure — possibly the place-name (cf. 1 Sam 4), possibly 'tribute to him' (shai lo) — so building chronology on an uncertain word is unsound. The messianic gloss in Onkelos identifies the ultimate referent without conceding any first-century deadline.

responseSource.name: Rashi and Ramban on Genesis 49:10; Tovia Singer, Outreach Judaism

rationale: Split verdict in practice: the messianic identification of Shiloh is admitted (Onkelos, Sanhedrin 98b, Rashi — cite them, they are common ground), but the popular Christian TIMING argument ('the scepter departed when the Sanhedrin lost capital cases, therefore Messiah had already come') is genuinely contested and half-broken — the Babylonian exile objection has no clean answer. Use the verse for what it firmly gives: Torah-level testimony, rabbinically confirmed, that Judah's line ends in one man who wins 'the obedience of the peoples' — then ask soberly which son of Judah the peoples of the earth actually obey. Drop the courtroom chronology entirely.

plain.d: Jacob is dying. He is blessing his twelve sons one by one. To Judah he says something odd. Genesis 49:10 keeps the ruler's staff with Judah "until Shiloh come." Then it adds: "unto him shall the gathering of the people be."

plain.t: Nobody is certain what Shiloh means
plain.d: Say that up front. It is one of the genuinely unclear words in the whole Old Testament. Suggested meanings include "the one it belongs to," a place name, and a title. Ancient Jewish translations read it as a name for the Messiah.

The verse ties Judah's ruling power to a deadline. So the question stops being about Hebrew and becomes about history: when did Judah's governing authority actually end? That is something the two of you can look up together.
Contested. The messianic reading is ancient and Jewish, which counts for a lot. The unclear word and the disputed history keep it from being settled.
It is one of the oldest passages Jewish readers treated as being about the Messiah. That was long before there was any argument with Christians about it.
"The Targum reads 'Shiloh' as the Messiah. What do you make of that?"

title: Isaiah 7:14 — almah, the Septuagint, and Matthew's typology (handle with care)
claim: Isaiah 7:14: 'The almah shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.' Matthew 1:23 cites it of the virgin birth via the Septuagint's parthenos. The honest facts: almah means a young woman of marriageable age (cf. Gen 24:43; Ex 2:8), not technically 'virgin' (betulah — though even betulah needs a qualifier in Gen 24:16); the sign is given to Ahaz with a near-term horizon — before the child knows good from evil, the two kings will be gone (7:15-16). What Christians CAN say: the choice of parthenos was made by Jewish translators in Alexandria two centuries before Jesus, so a virginal reading trajectory predates Christianity; the Immanuel child threads forward into 8:8-10 and the divine child of 9:6-7, suggesting a figure larger than the 8th-century sign; and Matthew's 'fulfill' (plēroō) regularly means typological filling-full of a pattern (Hos 11:1 in Matt 2:15 — Israel's exodus story recapitulated), not bare prediction.
rabbinic: Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 67 (Trypho's almah argument, 2nd c.)
response: The counter is ancient and strong — Trypho was already making it to Justin c. 160 AD: the Hebrew says almah, 'young woman'; the sign addresses Ahaz's crisis in 734 BC and is useless to him if fulfilled seven centuries later; verse 16 ties the child's early years to the fall of Rezin and Pekah; the child is plausibly Isaiah's or Ahaz's own son (cf. 8:3-4, where Maher-shalal-hash-baz carries the identical timetable). Parthenos in the LXX need not mean virgin technically (the violated Dinah is parthenos in Gen 34:3 LXX). Matthew, reading Greek, built doctrine on a translation choice. Later Jewish translators (Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion) rendered neanis, 'young woman' — correcting, not conspiring.

responseSource.name: Rashi on Isaiah 7:14; Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 67-71; Tovia Singer, Outreach Judaism

rationale: Graded contested, and the site should SAY Christians overclaim this verse — that honesty is the entry's main job. Isaiah 7:14 is not evidence FOR the virgin birth; it is Matthew's meditation ON a virgin birth he already believed on other grounds, using the accepted Jewish technique of pattern-fulfillment. Never open with it; never present it as a knockdown; if it comes up, concede the near-term fulfillment cheerfully and explain typology with Matthew 2:15 (Hosea 11:1), which no one can read as prediction. The defensible remainder: the LXX's parthenos shows the reading is pre-Christian, and the Immanuel-to-9:6 arc invites a larger horizon. Low weight, honestly held.

plain.d: Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." You have heard it read every December. It is also the weakest of the famous Christian proof-texts, and this page says so plainly.

The Hebrew word is almah. It means a young woman of marrying age. The specific Hebrew word for virgin is betulah, and Isaiah did not use it. So the English word "virgin" is carrying more weight than the Hebrew gives it.

Read the whole chapter. Isaiah is giving King Ahaz a sign about a war that was about to end. The child is a sign inside that crisis. A baby born seven hundred years later would not have helped Ahaz at all.

plain.t: What can still honestly be said
plain.d: Jewish translators — not Christians — rendered almah as parthenos, the Greek word for virgin, around 250 BC in the Septuagint. And Matthew is treating the verse as a pattern being filled out a second time, not as a one-meaning prediction.
Weak on its own. Use it as a pattern, or leave it alone. Giving this one away is exactly what earns you a hearing on Isaiah 53 and Daniel 9, which do hold.
"Honestly, I don't think this verse works the way it usually gets preached."

title: Messianic expectation was alive, specific, and datable before Jesus — 4Q521 and Psalms of Solomon
claim: The charge that Christians retrofitted a 'messiah concept' onto neutral texts fails on pre-Christian evidence. The Dead Sea Scroll 4Q521 (1st c. BC) says of the messianic age: 'the heavens and the earth will obey His Messiah... he will heal the badly wounded, he will revive the dead, he will proclaim good news to the poor' — strikingly close to Jesus's self-description to John the Baptist (Luke 7:22), including 'raises the dead,' which is NOT in the underlying Isaiah 35/61 texts. Psalms of Solomon 17 (mid-1st c. BC) prays for the 'son of David' who will reign as 'Lord Messiah.' Qumran expected priestly and royal anointed figures; Josephus records that an 'ambiguous oracle' in the scriptures convinced many the world ruler would arise from Judea in that era (War 6.312-313). Expectation was live, textual, and clustered exactly in Jesus's generation — the Gospels answer questions Second Temple Jews were already asking.

sources.name: Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library
John J. Collins, The Scepter and the Star
Craig Evans, Jesus and His Contemporaries

response: The response concedes the expectation but turns it: yes, first-century Judea was thick with messianic hope — which is precisely why there were MANY claimants (Theudas, the Egyptian, Bar Kokhba), all failed by the same test. The dominant expectation was a royal-national deliverer (Psalms of Solomon 17 is explicitly a conquering king who purges Jerusalem of gentiles); 4Q521's wonder-working figure is fragmentary and possibly describes God's own deeds, not the Messiah's. Jesus matched the marginal motifs and failed the central ones: no throne, no ingathering, no peace, no rebuilt temple — and the era's expectation itself, per Sanhedrin 97b, generated the very false-messiah problem the rabbis warned against.

responseSource.name: John J. Collins, The Scepter and the Star (on diversity of expectation); Maimonides, Melachim 11

rationale: The admitted fact — datable, pre-Christian, Jewish texts expecting an anointed one who heals, raises the dead, and preaches good news to the poor — is genuinely powerful, because Luke 7:22 shows Jesus answering John's 'are you the one?' in exactly that idiom. Use 4Q521 as the centerpiece: it cannot be a Christian forgery (it was sealed in a cave before the church existed). Concede the diversity of expectation and the failed-claimant field honestly; the argument is not 'expectation proves Jesus' but 'the messianic job description Christians cite was already posted.' Pairs naturally with the two-Messiah and Daniel 9 entries.

plain.d: A common claim is that Christians invented the Messiah they wanted, then read him backwards into the Old Testament. It sounds reasonable. It is also checkable, because we have Jewish writings from before Jesus was born.

plain.t: What the Dead Sea Scrolls show
plain.d: A scroll fragment called 4Q521 describes a Messiah under whom the blind see and the dead are raised. It is Jewish. It was written before Jesus. And it is almost word for word what Jesus later sends back to John the Baptist in Matthew 11:5.

The Psalms of Solomon, written roughly a century before Jesus, describe a king from David's line who cleanses Jerusalem and gathers the tribes. The expectation was alive, detailed, and datable. It was not made up afterwards.
Very strong. These are Jewish documents, dated by scholars who have no stake in the Christian conclusion.
It removes the "you invented it later" objection before it can be raised, using evidence that came out of a cave in 1947.
"Have you read 4Q521? It sounds a lot like Matthew 11, and it's older than Jesus."

title: Jeremiah 31: the 'new covenant' is the Tanakh's own promise — made to Israel
claim: The phrase 'new covenant' (brit chadashah) is not a Christian coinage — it appears once in the Tanakh, at Jeremiah 31:31-34 (31:30-33 in Hebrew editions): 'Behold, days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah — not like the covenant I made with their fathers... which they broke.' Its content: Torah written on hearts, everyone knowing the LORD, and — the climax — 'I will forgive their iniquity, and remember their sin no more.' The promise presupposes the Sinai covenant was breakable and was broken, and announces a covenant grounded in definitive forgiveness. The New Testament's entire self-understanding is a claim on this text: 'this cup is the new covenant in my blood' (Luke 22:20; 1 Cor 11:25), argued at length in Hebrews 8-10. Ezekiel parallels it (36:25-27, the new heart and Spirit). Whatever one concludes about Jesus, the category 'new covenant with Israel, centered on forgiveness' is Jeremiah's, not Paul's.

sources.name: Michael Brown, Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus, vol. 2

response: The rabbinic counter: read the CONTENT. The new covenant is the same Torah — 'I will put MY TORAH within them' — internalized so perfectly that it can no longer be broken; nothing here abolishes commandments, replaces Israel, or mentions a dying mediator. 'Chadashah' can mean renewed, as the moon is 'renewed.' Its timeframe is the messianic age, when 'they shall all know Me' — manifestly not the present era of a divided, largely unbelieving world. And the immediately following verses (31:35-37) stake God's own reliability on Israel's permanence as a nation 'forever' — the strongest anti-supersessionist text in the Bible, sitting inside the very passage Christians claim. If the church reads vv.31-34 literally, it must read vv.35-37 literally too.

responseSource.name: Rashi and Radak on Jeremiah 31; Tovia Singer, Outreach Judaism

rationale: Unrefuted on the narrow claim: the Tanakh itself anticipates a new covenant whose ground is final forgiveness, promised to Israel — Christians did not invent the category, they claim it. The counter succeeds only against the overreach (Torah abolished, Israel replaced) — which faithful use of this entry must also renounce. Deploy it double-edged, on purpose: yes, Jeremiah promised a new covenant (so considering the NT's claim is not apostasy from the Tanakh); and yes, vv.35-37 guarantee Israel forever (so any Christianity that despises Israel has broken with its own charter — cf. Romans 11). That symmetry is what makes this entry trustworthy to a Jewish reader.

plain.d: That Christianity invented a "new covenant" to replace the one God made with Israel. It gets said as though a new covenant were obviously a Christian idea, bolted on later to justify a new religion.

It is Jeremiah's. Jeremiah was a prophet in Jerusalem around 600 BC. He was writing to Jewish people. His book is part of the Hebrew Bible — what Christians call the Old Testament. So the phrase is not an import. It is already there.

plain.t: What the verse says, word for word
plain.d: Jeremiah 31:31 — "Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah." He names both. Not a different people. Those two.

plain.t: And what this new covenant does
plain.d: Jeremiah 31:33 says God will "put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts." Jeremiah 31:34 says everyone will know God directly. God will "remember their sin no more." A law inside people. Sins not just covered, but forgotten.
Strong. There is no good answer to it, because there is nothing to dispute. The words are in the Hebrew Bible and they name their own parties.

It stops an argument before it starts. Say your friend claims Christians invented a second covenant. You are not defending a Christian idea. You are asking about a promise their own prophet made. He made it in their Scriptures. He made it to their people. The question is no longer whether a new covenant was coming. It is only who brought it.
"Who is Jeremiah's new covenant made with? Read me Jeremiah 31:31."

title: Yoma 39b: the Temple's signs failed for the forty years before the destruction
claim: The Talmud itself records: 'Forty years before the destruction of the Temple, the lot ["For the LORD"] did not come up in the right hand; nor did the crimson-colored strap become white; nor did the westernmost lamp burn; and the doors of the Sanctuary opened by themselves' (Yoma 39b; parallel in Jerusalem Talmud Yoma 6:3). The crimson thread turning white was the visible sign that Yom Kippur's atonement had been accepted (per Isaiah 1:18, 'though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be white as snow'). The Temple fell in 70 AD; forty years earlier is approximately 30 AD — the era of the crucifixion. On the Christian reading, the rabbis' own tradition remembers that from roughly the moment Jesus died, the sacrificial system's acceptance-signs went dark, until the system itself ended. The same sugya frames the failures as divine displeasure, and Yochanan ben Zakkai reads the self-opening doors through Zechariah 11:1 as the Temple's doom.

sources.name: Michael Brown, Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus, vol. 1
Jacob Neusner, translations and studies of the Talmudic aggadah

response: The response: this is aggadah — homiletic memory, redacted centuries after the events, and 'forty years' is the Bible's and the Talmud's stock number for a generation (the wilderness, Eli, David); the same tractate says the thread's whitening had already become intermittent generations earlier, after Shimon HaTzaddik. The rabbis' own explanation for the withdrawal of favor is explicit and internal: the era's sins — notably baseless hatred (Yoma 9b) and the corruption of the late priesthood — not the rejection of a messianic claimant, which the sugya never mentions. Building chronology-dependent theology on a symbolic aggadic number, against its own stated context, is precisely the proof-texting Jews find in missionary literature.

responseSource.name: Standard rabbinic reading of Yoma 39b with Yoma 9b; counter-missionary treatments (Outreach Judaism)

rationale: Admitted, in the strict sense defined for this section: the text exists, is Jewish, and says what it says — divine acceptance-signs failed for the Temple's final forty years, a span that lands at ~30 AD. But the rationale must carry the honesty: this is suggestive convergence, not proof; the number is schematic; and the sugya's own theology blames communal sin, not Golgotha. Present it as a question the tradition leaves open — 'what happened around 30 AD that your own sources remember as the turning point?' — never as a checkmate. Overplaying Yoma 39b is a known missionary tic that Jewish readers are primed to distrust; underplay it and it lands harder.

plain.t: How the Day of Atonement worked
plain.d: Once a year the high priest drew lots between two goats. A crimson thread was said to turn white when the sacrifice was accepted. And a lamp in the Temple stayed lit as a sign that God was present. Everyone watched for those three signs.

A passage called Yoma 39b says that for the forty years before the Temple was destroyed, the signs stopped working. The lot no longer came up in the right hand. The thread stopped turning white. The westernmost lamp went out.
Rome destroyed the Temple in AD 70. Forty years before that is AD 30. That is the traditional date of the crucifixion.
Very strong, and you never have to argue for it. This is not a Christian source. It is one of Judaism's own central books, describing its own Temple, and nobody disputes that the passage says this.
You do not have to make a case at all. You only have to ask someone to read it and tell you what they think happened in AD 30.
"Would you look up Yoma 39b with me? I'd genuinely like to know how you read it."

title: Leviticus 17:11 and the vanished altar: what grounds atonement since 70 AD?
claim: Leviticus grounds atonement in substitutionary blood: 'the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls; for it is the blood that makes atonement by the life' (17:11). Yom Kippur's machinery is blood carried into the holy place (Lev 16). In 70 AD the altar vanished, and with it the entire biblically mandated apparatus of sacrificial atonement — nineteen centuries and counting. Rabbinic Judaism answered with substitutes: repentance, prayer, and charity. The Christian claim is that the timing is not accident but design: within one generation of Jesus's death — which the NT presents as the sacrifice the system prefigured (Heb 9-10; Isa 53:10, where the servant's life is an asham, a guilt offering) — God let the shadow-system end because the substance had come. Hosea's prophecy fits the shape of the age: 'many days without king... without sacrifice' before Israel returns and seeks 'David their king' (Hos 3:4-5).
rabbinic: Berakhot 26b (prayers instituted in place of sacrifices)

sources.name: Michael Brown, Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus, vol. 2
Jews for Judaism on atonement without sacrifice

response: The rabbinic counter is substantial and biblical: the Tanakh itself repeatedly shows atonement without blood. The poor bring a FLOUR sin-offering (Lev 5:11-13) — bloodless, yet 'the priest shall make atonement.' Hosea prescribes exile-piety: 'we will render the bulls of our lips' (14:2). Solomon's dedication prayer anticipates temple-less forgiveness through repentant prayer toward Jerusalem (1 Kings 8:46-50); Daniel prayed without a temple; Nineveh was forgiven by repentance alone (Jonah 3:10); 'the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit' (Ps 51:17); 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice' (Hos 6:6, cited by Yochanan ben Zakkai in ARN 4 — and by Jesus, Matt 9:13). Lev 17:11 addresses eating blood, not a universal atonement monopoly. God was never trapped in one mechanism.

responseSource.name: Avot deRabbi Natan 4; Tovia Singer, Outreach Judaism; Jews for Judaism

rationale: Graded contested because the rabbinic counter-case is real Bible, not evasion — flour offerings, Nineveh, and Psalm 51 must be conceded, and 'Judaism has no answer for sin' is a falsehood this site should kill. The genuine live question is narrower and worth posing with care: the Torah's own center of gravity for atonement — Yom Kippur, the altar, 'I have GIVEN it to you' — was blood and mediation; the substitutes were exilic accommodations the sources themselves frame as replacements (ARN 4 is a post-catastrophe consolation). Is a nineteen-century suspension of the Torah's central rite a footnote — or a signpost? Ask it as a question, in grief rather than triumph; this is the deepest disagreement, and the entry should feel its weight.

plain.t: What the law of Moses says
plain.d: Leviticus 17:11 is direct: "it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul." Atonement happens through blood placed on an altar. That altar stood in the Temple in Jerusalem, and nowhere else.
Rome destroyed the Temple in AD 70. It has never been rebuilt. So the one thing Leviticus names as the means of atonement has been gone for nineteen centuries.

With prayer, repentance and acts of kindness. This is a serious answer, worked out by people facing a catastrophe, and it has carried Judaism for a very long time. Treat it with respect or the conversation is over.
The Torah names blood on an altar. The rabbinic answer names something else. So: where does the Torah authorise the replacement? Ask it gently, once, and then stop talking.
Contested. The question is real and hard. The Jewish answer is not stupid, and treating it as stupid will end the conversation on the spot.
"Leviticus 17:11 grounds atonement in blood on an altar. What grounds it now?"

title: Israel's partial blindness and certain restoration — the frame that forbids contempt
claim: The Tanakh itself narrates a pattern for Israel: a long season without king or sacrifice, then wholehearted return — 'afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek the LORD their God and David their king in the latter days' (Hos 3:4-5); a spirit of deep sleep and sealed vision (Isa 29:10-14) that is lifted; scattering and regathering (Deut 30:1-6); the house of David looking on the pierced one and mourning, with a fountain opened for sin (Zech 12:10-13:1). Paul builds Romans 9-11 on exactly this pattern: Israel's present non-recognition of Jesus is 'partial and temporary' (Rom 11:25), engineered to bring the nations in, and it ends with 'all Israel will be saved' (11:26, citing Isa 59:20). The same chapter issues binding commands to gentile Christians: 'do not boast over the branches' (11:18), Israel remains 'beloved for the sake of the fathers,' and 'the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable' (11:28-29). Christian contempt for Jews is not a regrettable excess of the system — it is disobedience to the system's own charter.
rabbinic: Sanhedrin 97b-98a (redemption through repentance in the latter days)

sources.name: Romans 11 in context (NETS/NA28 via Bible Gateway)
Kendall Soulen, The God of Israel and Christian Theology
Michael Brown, Our Hands Are Stained with Blood

response: The Jewish response is not exegetical but historical, and it deserves full weight: whatever Romans 11 says, nineteen centuries of Christendom said otherwise — Justin claimed Israel's inheritance, Chrysostom preached against the synagogue, crusaders massacred Rhineland communities while Romans 11 sat in their Bibles, Luther's 'On the Jews and Their Lies' fed directly into 20th-century catastrophe. A charter that failed to restrain its own civilization for most of its history is fairly judged by its fruit (a test Jesus himself endorsed, Matt 7:16). Furthermore, 'all Israel will be saved' has itself been read supersessionistically ('Israel' = the church). A Jewish reader may reasonably conclude the text is at best ambiguous and at worst window-dressing.

responseSource.name: Jules Isaac, The Teaching of Contempt; standard Jewish historical critique of Christendom

rationale: Unrefuted at the textual level — Romans 11's plain sense condemns replacement contempt, and the history of its violation is a history of Christians breaking their own scripture, which the entry must say in those words. This is the posture-defining entry of the section: it goes FIRST in any real conversation. Practical use: open with confession, not citation — name the crusades, the blood libels, the Holy Week pogroms, the Shoah's Christian antecedents — and only then show that the NT's own charter (Rom 3:2's 'oracles of God were entrusted' to Israel; Rom 9:4-5; Rom 11) sides with the Jewish people against their persecutors. A Christian who will not grieve the history has no standing to open the texts.

plain.d: A Christian has to deal with what Christians have done. The Crusades. The blood libel — the lie that Jews murdered Christian children. The expulsions from England and Spain. Luther's writings. Then Christian Europe between 1941 and 1945.

Paul asks in Romans 11:1 whether God has cast away his people. He answers "God forbid." In Romans 11:29 he says God's calling of Israel "cannot be revoked." He describes the blindness as partial, and temporary, and ending.

Paul tells non-Jewish believers they are a branch grafted into someone else's tree. Then in Romans 11:18 he warns them directly: "boast not against the branches." The arrogance behind a thousand years of violence is condemned inside the New Testament itself.
Strong. There is no honest reading of Romans 11 that supports contempt. Christians who held one were reading against their own book.
Say this first, unprompted, before you open anything else. Your friend has probably spent their whole life waiting for a Christian who says it without being pushed into it.
"I know what the word Christian has meant to Jewish families. I'm not going to pretend otherwise."

title: The New Testament is a Jewish library — and modern Jewish scholarship reads it that way
claim: Every NT author except (probably) Luke was a Jew; its earliest community was a Torah-observant Jerusalem congregation of 'many thousands of Jews... all zealous for the law' (Acts 21:20). Matthew structures his Gospel in five great discourses echoing the Chumash and presents Jesus as the greater Moses who came 'not to abolish the Torah or the Prophets... but to fulfill' (Matt 5:17). Jesus's disputes — divorce, Sabbath healing, hand-washing — run along recognized Pharisaic fault lines (Hillel vs. Shammai). Paul calls himself a Pharisee in the present tense decades after Damascus (Acts 23:6; Phil 3:5) and argues halakhically from the Tanakh. This is now the mainstream of critical scholarship, much of it Jewish: Geza Vermes ('Jesus the Jew'), E.P. Sanders, Amy-Jill Levine and Marc Brettler's Jewish Annotated New Testament (Oxford), and Daniel Boyarin, who argues even the divine 'Son of Man' Messiah is a Jewish idea (Dan 7) before it is a Christian one. Reading the NT is reading an intra-Jewish argument of the first century.
rabbinic: Mishnah Gittin 9:10 (the Hillel/Shammai divorce dispute behind Matthew 19)

sources.name: The Jewish Annotated New Testament (Levine & Brettler, Oxford)

response: The response: Jewish authorship does not make a Jewish book — Spinoza was a Jew too. The NT as CANONIZED contains the seeds of the contempt: 'his blood be on us and on our children' (Matt 27:25), 'you are of your father the devil' (John 8:44), 1 Thess 2:14-16 — texts a Jewish reader encounters not as intra-Jewish rhetoric but as the proof-texts of pogroms. The 'parting of the ways' was real: whatever the first generation was, the church that transmitted these texts read them against the Jews for eighteen centuries. And theologically, the NT's claims — incarnation, a divine-human atoning mediator — cross lines (Deut 6:4; Num 23:19) that no amount of first-century Jewish context erases for rabbinic Judaism.

responseSource.name: Amy-Jill Levine (on hearing NT polemic with Jewish ears); standard rabbinic objections to incarnation

rationale: Admitted: the Jewishness of Jesus and the NT is now the consensus of critical scholarship, led substantially by Jewish scholars — cite Vermes, Levine, Boyarin, not apologists. Use this entry to change what the conversation IS: not 'convert to a gentile religion' but 'consider a first-century Jewish claim about a Jewish figure, made by Jews, from the Jewish scriptures.' Handle the response's charge without flinching: acknowledge that Matthew 27:25 and John 8:44 were weaponized, explain their first-century setting honestly, and grant that context does not undo centuries of hearing. Boyarin's Daniel 7 argument is the advanced move: divine-Messiah categories predate Christianity within Judaism itself.

plain.d: Many Jewish people meet the New Testament one way. It is the book of the religion that hurt their families. That makes it almost impossible to read as anything else. The reaction is earned.

Set the history aside for a moment and look at the books themselves. They were written almost entirely by Jews. They argue from the Hebrew Bible. They are about a Jewish teacher. They were written within a few decades, largely for Jewish readers.

Not Christian apologists. Amy-Jill Levine is a Jewish New Testament scholar. She helped edit the Jewish Annotated New Testament. Daniel Boyarin is another Jewish scholar. He argues that a divine, suffering Messiah was already a Jewish idea before Christianity.
Very strong. Jewish scholars are saying it, and they have no reason to want the Christian conclusion.

You are not asking anyone to stop being Jewish. The first followers of Jesus kept the feasts and argued from the Hebrew Bible in synagogues. That is a very different request from the one your friend is expecting.
"Have you seen Levine's Jewish Annotated New Testament? I'd be interested what you think of it."

title: DON'T USE: 'The Talmud says…' quote-mining and fabricated citations
claim: A body of fabricated or butchered 'Talmud quotes' has circulated for three centuries — Eisenmenger's Entdecktes Judentum (1700), August Rohling's Der Talmudjude (1871), Pranaitis's The Talmud Unmasked (1892), Elizabeth Dilling's The Plot Against Christianity (1964) — and now recycles endlessly online: invented references, mistranslations, censored-context passages alleging the Talmud blesses deceiving gentiles or blasphemes Jesus and Mary. At the 1913 Beilis blood-libel trial, Pranaitis was destroyed on cross-examination, unable to answer elementary Talmud questions. The genuine scholarly question of the few disputed 'Yeshu' passages is treated soberly in Peter Schäfer's Jesus in the Talmud (Princeton) — late, polemical-era texts of contested referent, censored under Christian pressure, telling us about medieval Jewish-Christian conflict, not first-century facts. Christians who traffic in Talmud memes are laundering antisemitic forgeries into an evangelistic conversation.
rabbinic: Peter Schäfer, Jesus in the Talmud (on the disputed Yeshu passages)

sources.name: Peter Schäfer, Jesus in the Talmud (Princeton UP)
ADL, resources on the Talmud in antisemitic polemics
Sefaria (read the actual texts in context)

response: No steelman exists for fabrication. The only honest residue: a handful of genuine Talmudic passages may polemicize against a figure some manuscripts call Yeshu; scholars dispute whether he is Jesus of Nazareth (chronological details conflict by a century). Even at maximum, they attest that late-antique Jews rejected Christian claims — which everyone already knew — and they were composed under persecution by the church, a context Christians created. Quoting them as ammunition is citing a community's wounded polemic while ignoring who wounded it.

responseSource.name: Peter Schäfer, Jesus in the Talmud; ADL documentation of fabricated quotes

rationale: Do not use — kill the practice by name. The eighth commandment applies to citations: a Christian who forwards a fabricated Talmud quote bears false witness against a neighbor, in Christ's name, in a genre with a body count (the Beilis trial, Nazi propaganda reprints of Rohling). If a Talmud passage matters to an argument, the rule is: read it on Sefaria, in context, with the standard commentaries, or do not cite it. This entry exists so the site can say plainly: the counter-missionary rabbis are RIGHT about this practice, and Christians should thank them for policing it.

plain.d: Lists of shocking quotations said to come from the Talmud. They are easy to find and they look damning. Do not use them.

Most are made up, mistranslated, or cut away from the words around them. The Talmud is a huge record of debate. It writes down the losing side of an argument next to the winning side. So a quotation can be the exact opposite of the ruling.
Most of these lists trace back to the Middle Ages. They were assembled for forced public debates, to justify what was done next. That is the company you keep when you repeat them.
If you cannot read the passage in context on Sefaria, do not use it. That check takes thirty seconds, and your friend can do it faster than you can.
If you have used one: "I repeated something about the Talmud once that turned out to be fake. I stopped doing that."

title: DON'T USE: the 'Jews killed Jesus' framing (deicide)
claim: The deicide charge is both theologically false by the NT's own account and historically the deadliest sentence in Christian rhetoric. The NT's account: crucifixion was a ROMAN penalty, executed by Roman soldiers under a Roman prefect's verdict; the Jewish participants were a narrow temple faction, not a people; Peter tells Jews in Jerusalem 'you acted in ignorance, as did your rulers' (Acts 3:17); the theological cause is the sin of all humanity within God's set plan — Acts 4:27-28 indicts Herod, Pilate, the gentiles AND Israel together, 'to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined'; Isaiah 53:10 says 'it pleased the LORD to crush him'; Jesus says 'no one takes my life from me — I lay it down of my own accord' (John 10:18). Historically, Matthew 27:25 read as a blood-curse underwrote Holy Week pogroms, expulsions, and blood libels for centuries — a legacy formally repudiated in Nostra Aetate §4 (1965): Christ's passion 'cannot be charged against all the Jews then alive, nor against the Jews of today.'
rabbinic: Nostra Aetate 4 (church document repudiating the charge)

sources.name: Jeremy Cohen, Christ Killers: The Jews and the Passion
Michael Brown, Our Hands Are Stained with Blood

response: There is no counter-argument to steelman — only the observation, which Jewish readers will rightly press, that the Gospels' passion narratives themselves (especially Matthew 27:25 and John's usage of 'the Jews') gave the charge its raw material, and that Christian theology cannot fully outsource the problem to 'misreaders.' A Christian using this framing has not merely erred tactically; he has contradicted his own scriptures and joined the persecutors' lineage.

responseSource.name: Jules Isaac, The Teaching of Contempt; Nostra Aetate

rationale: Do not use, ever, in any form — including softened versions ('your ancestors rejected him'). Theologically, the Christian confession is that MY sin required the cross; every communion liturgy says so. If the topic arises, the Christian's move is confession of the church's guilt for the deicide libel and its harvest of blood, followed if appropriate by Acts 4:27-28's actual theology of shared, predestined human responsibility. This entry exists to give the site's readers the exact language of repudiation and to mark the line: any 'Messiah case' that leans on collective Jewish guilt has already lost — biblically, historically, and morally.

plain.d: Most entries on this list are about losing an argument. This one is not. This is the specific claim that sat underneath a thousand years of killing.
The Rhineland massacres of 1096. The blood libel invented at Norwich in 1144 and repeated for centuries. Easter pogroms. Expulsions. And a vocabulary that was still in use in the twentieth century.

A Roman governor ordered the execution and Roman soldiers carried it out. The New Testament spreads the responsibility very differently — and in John 10:18 Jesus says plainly that nobody takes his life from him.
If any version of this phrase is in your vocabulary, take it out. Not softened. Out.
Nothing. This is one to never say — not one to say better.

title: DON'T USE: 'Judaism is legalistic works-righteousness'
claim: The caricature — Judaism as joyless rule-keeping to earn salvation, foil to Christian grace — is false on the sources and fatal to credibility. Rabbinic Judaism is saturated with grace: election precedes obligation ('All Israel has a share in the world to come,' Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1); the liturgy pleads 'Avinu Malkeinu, be gracious to us and answer us, for we have no deeds' (chonneinu va'aneinu ki ein banu ma'asim); the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy (Ex 34:6-7) anchor the High Holy Days; chesed (covenant love) is arguably the Tanakh's central divine attribute. E.P. Sanders's Paul and Palestinian Judaism (1977) demolished the caricature academically, coining 'covenantal nomism': Jews keep Torah as covenant response to a gracious God, not as wage labor for salvation — a structure formally like Christian obedience. The REAL disagreement, which this site should state precisely, is not grace vs. works but the GROUND of atonement: whether repentance suffices, or whether God has provided a mediating sacrifice (Lev 17:11; Isa 53) in the Messiah.

sources.name: E.P. Sanders, Paul and Palestinian Judaism
The Jewish Annotated New Testament (essays on Paul and Judaism)

response: The only pushback worth noting runs the other way: some scholars (the 'new perspective' debate) argue Sanders overcorrected and that Second Temple sources do contain merit-weighing strands (e.g., 4 Ezra). True but irrelevant to the practice this entry bans: whatever the academic balance, telling a Jewish friend her religion is loveless legalism is false about the Judaism she actually lives — her Shabbat table, her liturgy of mercy, her grandmother's chesed — and instantly identifies the speaker as someone who has never read a page of the siddur.

responseSource.name: E.P. Sanders, Paul and Palestinian Judaism; new-perspective literature (Dunn, Wright) and critics

rationale: Do not use. It fails academically (Sanders), liturgically (Avinu Malkeinu), and relationally (it insults the hearer's lived experience). It also misreads Paul, whose argument in Romans 9-10 is about Israel's relationship to the Messiah, not about Jews lacking grace. Replace it with the honest fault line this section is built on: both traditions know grace and repentance; they divide over whether atonement finally requires the mediating sacrifice the Torah's own cult embodied — which is a real, respectful, biblical conversation instead of a slander.

plain.d: That Judaism is about earning God's favour by keeping rules, and that Jesus and Paul replaced that with grace. It is a tidy story. It is also wrong.

E. P. Sanders took this apart in 1977 and the field moved. Judaism in Jesus's day was a religion of covenant grace with obligations. You are in because God chose you, and you live accordingly. That is closer to the New Testament than the caricature is.
Repeating it tells your Jewish friend you have never actually asked them what they believe. You are arguing with a cartoon, and they can hear it immediately.
Ask. You will learn something true, and you will be trusted with the answer.
"What do you actually believe about how a person stands right with God?"

title: DON'T USE: gematria proofs and Bible codes
claim: Arguments from equidistant letter sequences ('Yeshua encoded in Isaiah 53'), gematria equivalences, and Torah-code 'discoveries' should be banned from the Messiah case. The flagship academic claim (Witztum, Rips & Rosenberg, Statistical Science 1994) was formally answered by McKay, Bar-Natan, Bar-Hillel & Kalai, 'Solving the Bible Code Puzzle' (Statistical Science 14.2, 1999, 150-173), which showed the result 'fatally defective' — an artifact of flexible data selection. Answering journalist Michael Drosnin's challenge, McKay 'found' the Rabin assassination and other encoded prophecies in Moby-Dick. The method proves anything, therefore nothing: with enough freedom in spelling, skip distance, and appellation choice, any text of sufficient length yields any message. Christian use of codes borrows the least defensible fringe of Jewish mysticism to prop up a case that — as the rest of this section shows — can stand on the plain text, the Targums, and the Talmud read in context.
nt: Luke 24:27 (Jesus argues from the plain scriptures, 'in all the scriptures')
rabbinic: Witztum-Rips-Rosenberg, Statistical Science 1994 (the original ELS claim)

sources.name: McKay et al., 'Solving the Bible Code Puzzle,' Statistical Science 14.2 (1999)
Brendan McKay's Torah codes refutation pages (incl. Moby-Dick 'codes')
Semantic Scholar record of the debate

response: Defenders (Witztum's replies, the Meru Foundation) argue McKay's counter-experiments used looser rules than the original and that some ELS phenomena survive. But the methodological point is conceded even by sympathetic statisticians: results are exquisitely sensitive to researcher degrees of freedom, unfalsifiable in practice, and reproducible in secular control texts. No rabbinic authority rests doctrine on codes, and classical gematria (e.g., in Baal HaTurim) is homiletic ornament, never proof — a distinction the tradition itself maintains.

responseSource.name: McKay, Bar-Natan, Bar-Hillel & Kalai, Statistical Science 1999; Witztum's rejoinders

rationale: Do not use. Codes and gematria invert this section's whole epistemology: the Messiah case claims the PLAIN sense of public texts — the same verses the Targums and Talmud discuss — read the way Jesus himself argued 'from Moses and all the prophets' (Luke 24:27). Hidden-message arguments concede that the plain text is insufficient, collapse under statistics, and associate the gospel with Drosnin-grade sensationalism. If a reader arrives via a codes video, this entry redirects: the interesting question was never letter-skips in Isaiah 53 — it is what Isaiah 53 says.

plain.d: Gematria gives Hebrew letters number values and adds them up. Bible codes claim that skipping letters at fixed intervals spells out hidden messages. Both get used in Christian outreach as if they were evidence.

Researchers ran the same methods on Moby-Dick and War and Peace. They produced equally striking "predictions," including assassinations. Any long book will do this, because the method finds patterns instead of testing them.
Using them tells a thoughtful person that you cannot tell a pattern from a proof. Every real argument you make afterwards gets quietly discounted.
Drop them. The case from Isaiah 53, Daniel 9 and Yoma 39b does not need help from number games, and is weakened by standing next to them.
"I don't use the Bible-codes material. I don't think it holds up, and it isn't needed."
